questions.q: What makes timeliness different from the other five dimensions covered in this chapter?
options: It measures the data's relationship to time rather than a property of the value itself
It is the only dimension that cannot be checked with SQL
It only applies to numeric columns
It is a synonym for accuracy
questions.explain: Accuracy, completeness, consistency, validity, and uniqueness all evaluate the data itself. Timeliness evaluates whether the data still reflects reality closely enough in time, independent of whether the value is otherwise correct.

questions.q: What is the difference between freshness and latency?
options: Freshness measures how old data is relative to its expected update cadence; latency measures the delay between an event happening and it appearing in the system
Freshness and latency are two names for the exact same measurement
Freshness applies only to text columns; latency applies only to numeric columns
Latency can only be measured once a day; freshness can be measured continuously
questions.explain: Freshness is about the data's age relative to how often it should update. Latency is about the gap between a real-world event and that event being reflected in the system — a pipeline-speed measurement, not an age measurement.

questions.q: Why can a perfectly accurate value still fail a timeliness check?
options: The value may have been true when captured, but the real-world fact it represents may have since changed
Timeliness checks always flag accurate values as a false positive
Accuracy and timeliness are measured with incompatible data types
SQL Server cannot evaluate timestamp columns
questions.explain: A value's accuracy doesn't degrade in the database, but the real-world fact behind it can change over time — a shipping address captured correctly a year ago may no longer be current, which is a timeliness, not accuracy, problem.

questions.q: In the latency example query, which two columns does the check need in order to measure latency?
options: A timestamp for when the event actually happened and a timestamp for when it was loaded into the system
Only a single LastUpdated timestamp column
A primary key and a foreign key column
A Status column and a Quantity column
questions.explain: Latency requires comparing two timestamps — OrderPlacedAt (when the real-world event occurred) and LoadedIntoWarehouseAt (when it arrived in the target system) — to compute the delay between them.

questions.q: What determines the 'right' freshness threshold (like the 24-hour cutoff in the lesson's example)?
options: The business's actual expectation for how often that specific data should be updated
A fixed value built into SQL Server that applies to every table
Whichever threshold produces the fewest flagged rows
The data type of the LastUpdated column
questions.explain: The lesson notes the threshold depends entirely on how often the business expects the data to change, not on a technical default — deliberately setting that threshold is covered in Lesson 21.
